title: Cartan and raising operators on the free associative word space
statement:
Let $I$ be a finite set, $B=(b_{ij})_{i,j\in I}$ any rational matrix, and $\lambda=(\lambda_i)_{i\in I}\in\mathbf Q^I$. Let $A(I)$ be the rational vector space with basis all finite words in $I$, including the empty word $1$. For a basis word $w=(j_1,\ldots,j_m)$ set $\beta_i(w)=\sum_{r=1}^m b_{i j_r}$, with $\beta_i(1)=0$. For $j\in I$, let $t_jw$ denote the word obtained by prepending $j$, and extend this operation linearly. Define rational linear endomorphisms $F_i,H_i,E_i$ of $A(I)$ by their values on basis words:
$$F_i(w)=t_iw,\qquad H_i(w)=(\lambda_i-\beta_i(w))w,$$
$$E_i(1)=0,\qquad E_i(t_jw)=t_jE_i(w)+\delta_{ij}(\lambda_i-\beta_i(w))w.$$
The recursion terminates by word length. With the commutator Lie bracket on $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbf Q}(A(I))$ [def-wf-lie-algebra], these operators satisfy, for every $i,j\in I$,
$$[H_i,H_j]=0,\quad [E_i,F_j]=\delta_{ij}H_i,\quad [H_i,E_j]=b_{ij}E_j,\quad [H_i,F_j]=-b_{ij}F_j.$$
There is no restriction on the diagonal, signs or rank of $B$, and $I$ may be empty.

proof.text: Construct the basis values of $E_i$ by induction on length: the empty word has value zero, and the displayed rule at $t_jw$ uses only the already constructed value at the shorter word $w$. At each stage the result is a finite linear combination of words. Extend these values, and those of $F_i,H_i$, by linearity to $A(I)$; uniqueness follows because every vector is a finite linear combination of basis words. Directly from the finite sum defining the weights, $\beta_i(t_jw)=b_{ij}+\beta_i(w)$ for every $w$, including $w=1$.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, first proof, printed p.504: supporting word-operator construction; the following explicit calculation is supplied by Q103, not stated in Milne. Bourbaki VIII, §4, no.2 remains WANTED.

proof.text: Use the commutator convention $[X,Y]=XY-YX$ of [def-wf-lie-algebra]. On a basis word $w$, the two composites $H_iH_j$ and $H_jH_i$ both give $(\lambda_i-\beta_i(w))(\lambda_j-\beta_j(w))w$, since rational scalars commute. Thus $[H_i,H_j]=0$ by linearity.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, first proof, printed p.504: supporting word-operator construction; the following explicit calculation is supplied by Q103, not stated in Milne. Bourbaki VIII, §4, no.2 remains WANTED.

proof.text: On every basis word $w$, the defining recursion gives $E_iF_j(w)=F_jE_i(w)+\delta_{ij}(\lambda_i-\beta_i(w))w$. Subtract $F_jE_i(w)$ and use the definition of $H_i$ to obtain $[E_i,F_j](w)=\delta_{ij}H_i(w)$. The same identity holds on all vectors by linearity, with bracket as in [def-wf-lie-algebra].

proof.text: The weight identity of step 1 gives $H_iF_j(w)=(\lambda_i-\beta_i(w)-b_{ij})t_jw$, whereas $F_jH_i(w)=(\lambda_i-\beta_i(w))t_jw$. Subtraction yields $[H_i,F_j](w)=-b_{ij}F_j(w)$ and hence the endomorphism identity, using the commutator definition of [def-wf-lie-algebra].

source.place: Theorem 23.63, first proof, printed p.504: supporting word-operator construction; the following explicit calculation is supplied by Q103, not stated in Milne. Bourbaki VIII, §4, no.2 remains WANTED.

proof.text:
Fix $i,j$ and put $D=H_iE_j-E_jH_i$. Prove $D(w)=b_{ij}E_j(w)$ by induction on the length of the basis word $w$. At $w=1$, both sides vanish since $E_j(1)=0$ and $H_i(1)=\lambda_i1$. For the step write the word as $F_kw$, and set $\delta=\delta_{jk}$. Steps 3 and 4, valid on every vector, give $E_jF_k=F_kE_j+\delta H_j$ and $H_iF_k=F_kH_i-b_{ik}F_k$. Expanding both terms of $D(F_kw)$ with these two equations gives
$$D(F_kw)=F_kD(w)-b_{ik}F_kE_j(w)+\delta H_iH_j(w)-\delta H_jH_i(w)+b_{ik}E_jF_k(w).$$
By step 2 the middle Cartan difference is zero, and step 3 reduces the remaining two terms to $\delta b_{ik}H_j(w)$. Apply the induction hypothesis and $\delta_{jk}b_{ik}=\delta_{jk}b_{ij}$ (check $j=k$ and $j\ne k$) to get
$$D(F_kw)=b_{ij}F_kE_j(w)+\delta b_{ij}H_j(w)=b_{ij}E_jF_k(w).$$
This completes the induction and, by linearity and [def-wf-lie-algebra], proves $[H_i,E_j]=b_{ij}E_j$.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, first proof, printed p.504: supporting word-operator construction; the following explicit calculation is supplied by Q103, not stated in Milne. Bourbaki VIII, §4, no.2 remains WANTED.

proof.text: The four identities have now been proved for every pair of indices. Each calculation used only the displayed rational coefficients and the word recursion: no symmetry, sign, rank or diagonal condition on $B$ was introduced. If $I$ is empty, its only word is $1$, so $A(I)=\mathbf Q1$; there are no indexed operators or pairs of indices, and all four universal assertions are vacuous.
